name: Manometer
seoDesc: Manometer: work out atmospheric pressure from the gauge pressure at B and the density. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Manometer calculator the gauge pressure at B, the density and the height difference of A and B and it returns atmospheric pressure. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Manometer calculator work?
sections.html:
The Manometer calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports atmospheric pressure in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the manometer type and number of fluids); then you type in the gauge pressure at B (Fluid pressure), the density (ρ₁), the height difference of A and B (h₁) and the gauge Pressure at B.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Manometer calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Atmospheric pressure=absolute pressure at point A + density (ρ) × gravitational acceleration (g) × height of liquid (h)
Gauge pressure at C=density (ρ₃) × gravitational acceleration (g) × height difference of C and D (h₃) + gauge pressure at D
Gauge pressure at B=density (ρ₁) × gravitational acceleration (g) × height difference of A and B (h₁)
Is point B above C?=(-gauge pressure at B + gauge pressure at C) ÷ (density (ρ₂) × gravitational acceleration (g) × height difference of B and C (h₂))
Is point A above point B?=gauge pressure at B ÷ (density (ρ₁) × gravitational acceleration (g) × height difference of A and B (h₁))
Density (ρ₂)=(gauge pressure at B − gauge pressure at C) ÷ (gravitational acceleration (g) × height difference of B and C (h₂))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Pressure, opening in pascals

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Manometer calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the gauge pressure at B, the density and the height difference of A and B — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Manometer calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns atmospheric pressure, derived from the gauge pressure at B, the density and the height difference of A and B. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Manometer calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the gauge pressure at B, the density and the height difference of A and B, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter gravitational acceleration (g) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Gravitational acceleration (g) opens in meters per second squared and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Manometer calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
